paragraphs.text: Owen put the parcel beside the umbrella stand. His eyes went from the parcel to the carpet, then settled somewhere between them. He shifted the position of his hands and took in the room once more. Upstairs, his aunt called that supper would be ready when the potatoes had softened.

Mara kept glancing above the cashier's shoulder. The security mirror showed a man opening her unattended backpack near the entrance. She left her groceries on the belt, pointed him out to the guard, and ran back before he could pull the bag's padded camera insert free.

Tomas arrived at the farmhouse with a box of nails and the blue tarpaulin his cousin had requested. He set both on the porch, out of the rain. There was a little interval of stillness; his eyes rested, moved, and rested again, while his shoulders made their small adjustment to the moment. His cousin came around from the shed carrying a ladder. Together they took the tarpaulin upstairs and spread it beneath the hole where the roof tiles had slipped during the night.

Before answering the invitation, Bea turned the card over and traced the handwriting with her finger. The loops matched the notes her mother used to leave in her schoolbag; the signature on the front belonged to someone else. She fetched an old note from the biscuit tin and held the two beside each other. Then she rang the number on the invitation and asked who had addressed the envelope. The woman who answered said that Bea's mother had been helping at the church office.

The ferry clerk laid a timetable between us and asked which island I wanted. I gave my eyes a moment to travel, let them come to rest, and adjusted myself against the feeling of the pause. A child behind me was tapping a coin against the counter. I asked for the earliest crossing to the northern island, the one with the old quarry. The clerk circled a departure in red and explained that I would have to change boats at the harbor on the mainland.

I watched the cashier's hands rather than her face because she was counting my change into two piles. One pile covered the purchase and the other replaced a damaged note I had handed in earlier. When she pushed both piles forward, I checked them separately against the two receipts before leaving.

Their eyes traveled from the window to the floor. A bowl of wrapped sweets occupied the sideboard, and a square of afternoon light lay across the woven rug beside it.
